title: The system: an airline operations event platform on Kafka
caption: Three sources write to one replicated log; a stream processor joins delays with bookings, and four consumer groups read the same records for different jobs, each at its own pace.

steps.text: Flight-ops publishes every status change (a delay, a gate change, a cancellation) to flight-status, keyed by flight leg (flight number + date), so all events of one leg stay in order on one partition. The record carries a schema id the registry has approved.

Bookings get no second write path: a CDC connector tails the bookings database's change log and publishes one record per booked segment (passenger × leg) to the bookings topic, re-keyed from the booking id to the same leg id by a key transform.

Crew scheduling publishes duty assignments to crew-duty. Every topic has 3 replicas. With acks=all a write is acknowledged once every in-sync replica has it, and refused if fewer than 2 are in sync (min.insync.replicas=2).

The stream processor joins delays with bookings. Both topics use the same key and partition count, so a leg's delay and its bookings land on the same task. When a delay leaves a connection shorter than the minimum connecting time, it writes the passenger to misconnects.

Four consumer groups read the same log, each with its own committed offsets: notifications (status + misconnects), display boards (status), crew re-planning (status + crew-duty) and the analytics sink (everything).
Each group works at its own pace: notifications call the push and SMS vendors, the sink writes hourly files to the lake. A slow group only falls behind itself; nobody else waits for it.

scenarios.name: Storm at a hub
scenarios.summary: Thunderstorms close a hub for two hours: status events jump about 40×, and the log absorbs the burst while each group catches up at its own speed.

steps.text: Within ten minutes several hundred legs are delayed or re-gated, many of them more than once. Flight-ops publishes all of it.
Because the key is the leg, not the airport, the burst spreads over all 24 partitions of flight-status instead of melting one.
Each delay joins with that leg's bookings: tens of thousands of misconnected passengers are written back to Kafka in a few minutes.

Notifications lag by minutes, so its group scales out towards one member per partition. Boards and crew re-planning do little work per event and stay current; per-group lag alerts show exactly who is behind.

scenarios.name: SMS vendor outage
scenarios.summary: One downstream dependency fails: only the group that needs it falls behind, and it resumes from its committed offsets without losing a message.

steps.text: The SMS vendor starts timing out. Notifications can't send, so it retries with backoff and stops committing offsets past the messages it hasn't sent.
Its lag grows for the 20 minutes of the outage. The records are safe in the log: retention is 7 days, far longer than any vendor outage.
Display boards, crew re-planning and the sink read the same partitions at their own offsets and never notice.
The vendor recovers and notifications drain the backlog. A few messages were sent just before a timeout, so the sender dedupes on (passenger, event id) to avoid a second SMS.

scenarios.name: New schema field
scenarios.summary: Flight-ops adds a delay reason: the registry checks the change before it ships, and old consumers keep working.

steps.text: Flight-ops adds an optional delay_reason field with a default and registers schema version 2. The registry checks it is backward compatible and accepts it.
A change that renamed the gate field would have been rejected right there, at deploy time, before any consumer read a single record.
New records carry the v2 schema id. Display boards still read them with v1 and ignore the field; notifications upgrade when they want to show the reason.
